issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the concurrent findings of the Trial Court, Sessions Court, and the High Court, which upheld the order issuing summons against the appellant for the alleged offences.

application.point: The Supreme Court noted that three lower courts—the Trial Court, the Sessions Court, and the High Court—had all previously examined the case and upheld the decision to issue summons.
snippet: In view of the said observations made and prima facie findings recorded by the three courts below as regards the alleged involvement of the appellant in the alleged offences, this Court is not inclined to interfere with the same.

application.point: The Court observed that the lower courts had conducted a detailed and thorough review. The Trial Court meticulously examined the complaint and evidence, showing "proper application of mind" by issuing summons for some offences while dismissing others. The Sessions Court and High Court also dealt with every aspect of the matter in detail.
snippet: The Trial court after meticulously examining the allegations made in the complaint and the evidence of the complainant and one witness, had taken the cognizance, with regard to the aforesaid offences only and had not taken cognizance of the other offences alleged... which shows proper application of mind by the Trial Court...

The Sessions Court in the Revision petitions filed by the appellant had also upheld the said orders passed by the trial court issuing summons against the appellant and others after dealing with each and every aspect of the matter...
The High Court in the impugned order has also discussed in detail the submissions made by the counsels for the parties...

application.point: The Supreme Court acknowledged that summoning an accused is a serious matter that requires careful scrutiny to prevent frivolous complaints. However, it balanced this with the need to prosecute individuals against whom grave allegations are made.
snippet: No doubt, summoning of an accused is a serious matter and therefore the Magistrate before issuing the summons to the accused is obliged to scrutinize carefully the allegations made in the complaint with a view to prevent a person named therein as accused from being called upon to face any frivolous complaint, nonetheless one of the objects of Section 202 Cr.P.C. is also to enable the Magistrate to prosecute a person or persons against whom grave allegations are made.

application.point: After its own careful examination of the record, the Supreme Court found no "illegality or infirmity" in the orders passed by the lower courts.
snippet: Suffice it to say that having carefully examined the record of the complaints in question, we do not find any illegality or infirmity in the orders passed by the trial court issuing summons against the appellant-Archbishop for the alleged offences.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal and refused to interfere with the summons, holding that there was no illegality or infirmity in the concurrent findings of the three lower courts. These courts had all conducted a detailed review and found a prima facie case for the appellant's involvement in the alleged offences, justifying the issuance of the summons.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in invoking its suo motu jurisdiction and passing a series of subsequent orders after dismissing the main petitions filed under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C.

facts: After dismissing the main petitions filed under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., the High Court invoked its suo motu jurisdiction.

The High Court then passed a series of subsequent orders directing the State Government to inquire into property sales, advising the government to legislate a new law, and impleading the CBI as a respondent in the already disposed-of case.
The concerned judge retained the matters even after a change of roster and continued to pass orders on issues that were not the subject matter of the original petitions.
law: Courts must exercise their jurisdiction, including the inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and writ jurisdiction under Article 226, within the defined scope and ambit of the law.
Judicial enthusiasm for doing substantial justice must be tempered by judicial restraint and cannot cross the boundaries of judicial activism.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had adopted an "overzealous approach" and had "travelled not only beyond the scope and ambit of Section 482 Cr.P.C and of Article 226 of the Constitution of India, but had crossed all the boundaries of judicial activism and judicial restraint."

The High Court's actions, such as directing inquiries and advising on legislation on matters not argued or presented in the original petitions, were taken under the "guise of doing real and substantial justice" but were improper once the main case was disposed of.
The Supreme Court characterized these subsequent orders as "unwarranted."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in invoking its suo motu jurisdiction and passing subsequent orders after the main petitions had been dismissed. Consequently, the Supreme Court quashed and set aside all of these subsequent orders.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power of judicial review must be exercised by High Courts within permissible legal limits and in accordance with well-recognized judicial principles, and cannot be based on the personal predilections of individual judges or a sense of self-righteousness that overawes other authorities discharging their statutory functions.
obiter: Unwarranted judicial activism may cause uncertainty or confusion not only in the mind of the authorities but also in the mind of the litigants.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the appeal against the summons was dismissed, the Court found that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by passing a series of suo motu orders after the main petitions were already disposed of. The High Court's actions constituted unwarranted judicial activism that crossed the boundaries of its powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and Article 226 of the Constitution.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that the power to do substantial justice must be applied by courts within permissible legal limits.
The jurisdictional limits imposed by Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

policy_considerations: Judicial restraint is a virtue, and the predilections of individual judges, howsoever well intentioned, cannot be permitted to be operated in utter disregard of the well-recognized judicial principles governing uniform application of law.
The belief of self-righteousness or smugness of the High Court in exercise of its powers of judicial review should not overawe the other authorities discharging their statutory functions.
Unwarranted judicial activism may cause uncertainty or confusion not only in the mind of the authorities but also in the mind of the litigants.
